anchor-cycle.prompt: A clean 16:9 textbook diagram designed for legibility at 480p. White background, flat pastel fills, navy outlines, no gradients. Across the top, the exact title "Citric acid cycle" in large navy lettering. Below, a broad peach mitochondrial cutaway with two membranes and sparse folded cristae around its edges; the pale cream matrix contains a large clockwise pathway loop. The pathway is clearly a symbolic diagram, not a physical circular organelle structure. Eight pale rectangular molecule panels surround the loop: "Oxaloacetate" at upper left, "Citrate" at upper right, "Isocitrate" at right upper-middle, "α-Ketoglutarate" at right lower-middle, "Succinyl-CoA" at bottom right, "Succinate" at bottom left, "Fumarate" at left lower-middle, and "Malate" at left upper-middle. Use readable 18-pixel-equivalent navy labels on opaque cream panels, with the longest name wrapped across two lines without changing its spelling. An entry arrow labeled "Acetyl-CoA" leads into the oxaloacetate-to-citrate reaction. A small outgoing "CoA-SH" tab sits beside that entry. At the isocitrate-to-alpha-ketoglutarate reaction, outgoing tags read "CO₂" and "NADH". At the alpha-ketoglutarate-to-succinyl-CoA reaction, outgoing tags again read "CO₂" and "NADH". At the succinyl-CoA-to-succinate reaction, outgoing tags read "CoA-SH" and "GTP → ATP". At the succinate-to-fumarate reaction, a tag reads "FADH₂"; place a small plain blue membrane-contact marker beside this reaction without lettering it. At the malate-to-oxaloacetate reaction, a tag reads "NADH". All product tags have navy lettering and pale blue backing. Leave generous spacing between tags and panels. No atom identities, extra words, reaction numbers, legend, or decorative lettering. This is the complete layout master; the animation will hide labels until their corresponding reaction occurs.

brief: Make a 60-second widescreen explainer video on the citric acid cycle (the Krebs cycle) for first-year biology students. Show the cycle as a loop inside a mitochondrion: acetyl-CoA enters and joins oxaloacetate to form citrate, two carbons leave as CO2, NADH, FADH2 and ATP are produced along the way, and oxaloacetate is regenerated so the loop starts again. Label the key molecules on screen as they appear, under the title 'Citric acid cycle'. Calm English narration explaining each step as it happens. Simple clean 2D animation, no music.

research.subject: Citric acid cycle — research for one complete turn inside a mitochondrion, rather than a historical discovery episode. Follow acetyl-group entry, energy capture, carbon dioxide release and oxaloacetate regeneration. Dates below identify source publication dates, not dates when these recurring biochemical reactions occurred. The 60-second running time is a presentation choice, not the measured duration of one turn.

looks.look: The textbook describes oval-shaped organelles with two membranes. The inner membrane folds into cristae; the matrix occupies the space inside that membrane. Figure 4.14 provides an electron-micrograph reference. These documented features support a simplified cutaway; the source does not establish natural animation colors. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells))

Figure 7.11 depicts eight numbered reactions connected by arrows in a closed loop, with acetyl-CoA entering near oxaloacetate. This is a pathway diagram, not a literal circular structure inside the mitochondrion. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/apps/image-cdn/v1/f%3Dwebp/apps/archive/20260604.144757/resources/a84c5164820430e4fbb277e533da26ccdbba5490))

The reference figure shows acetyl-CoA as a condensed chemical structure with its acetyl group attached to S-CoA. CoA-SH is separately labeled when released. These are symbolic chemical representations, not documented visible shapes or colors of individual molecules. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/apps/image-cdn/v1/f%3Dwebp/apps/archive/20260604.144757/resources/a84c5164820430e4fbb277e533da26ccdbba5490))

looks.thing: Oxaloacetate, citrate, isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, succinate, fumarate and malate
looks.look: Figure 7.11 presents each intermediate as a named, condensed chemical structure in a pale rectangular panel. Its structures distinguish the carbon skeletons and functional groups. Use these as diagram references rather than inventing realistic molecular appearances. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/apps/image-cdn/v1/f%3Dwebp/apps/archive/20260604.144757/resources/a84c5164820430e4fbb277e533da26ccdbba5490))

looks.thing: NAD⁺/NADH, FAD/FADH₂, GDP/GTP, ADP/ATP, phosphate, water, hydrogen ions and CO₂
looks.look: The reference figure uses abbreviated labels beside reaction arrows rather than detailed molecular models. NADH appears at three positions, FADH₂ at one, and CO₂ at two; GTP formation is linked to ATP formation. These are documented graphic conventions, not natural appearances. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/apps/image-cdn/v1/f%3Dwebp/apps/archive/20260604.144757/resources/a84c5164820430e4fbb277e533da26ccdbba5490))

The source documents its position embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, unlike the soluble cycle enzymes. It does not establish a particular silhouette or color; do not present an invented enzyme icon as a verified molecular shape. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/biology/pages/7-3-oxidation-of-pyruvate-and-the-citric-acid-cycle))

facts.fact: In eukaryotic cells, the cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. Succinate dehydrogenase is the exception to the soluble cycle enzymes: it is embedded in the inner membrane. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/biology/pages/7-3-oxidation-of-pyruvate-and-the-citric-acid-cycle))
facts.when: Source published October 21, 2016; recurring biochemical process.

facts.fact: Acetyl-CoA supplies a two-carbon acetyl group, which joins four-carbon oxaloacetate to form six-carbon citrate. Coenzyme A is released; the whole acetyl-CoA molecule does not become citrate. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/7-3-oxidation-of-pyruvate-and-the-citric-acid-cycle))

Citrate is rearranged into isocitrate, retaining six carbons. This supplies the next labeled intermediate before carbon dioxide release begins. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/7-3-oxidation-of-pyruvate-and-the-citric-acid-cycle))

Isocitrate becomes five-carbon α-ketoglutarate, releasing one CO₂ and producing the first NADH. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/7-3-oxidation-of-pyruvate-and-the-citric-acid-cycle))

α-Ketoglutarate becomes four-carbon succinyl-CoA. A second CO₂ leaves, and a second NADH is produced. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/7-3-oxidation-of-pyruvate-and-the-citric-acid-cycle))

Succinyl-CoA becomes succinate, releasing CoA and generating one GTP or ATP, depending on cell type. For the requested ATP display, a GTP → ATP callout matches the textbook diagram without implying both are additional net products. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/biology/pages/7-3-oxidation-of-pyruvate-and-the-citric-acid-cycle))

Succinate becomes fumarate as FAD is reduced to FADH₂. Fumarate then becomes malate through addition of water. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/biology/pages/7-3-oxidation-of-pyruvate-and-the-citric-acid-cycle))
facts.when: Source published October 21, 2016; sixth and seventh reactions.

facts.fact: Malate becomes oxaloacetate, generating the third NADH. Regenerated oxaloacetate can accept another acetyl group, completing the loop. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/7-3-oxidation-of-pyruvate-and-the-citric-acid-cycle))
facts.when: Source published March 28, 2018; eighth reaction and restart.

facts.fact: Each turn yields two CO₂, three NADH, one FADH₂ and one ATP equivalent. NADH and FADH₂ connect the cycle to subsequent ATP production through the electron-transport pathway. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/concepts-biology/pages/4-3-citric-acid-cycle-and-oxidative-phosphorylation?utm_source=openai))
facts.when: Source published April 25, 2013; accounting per complete turn.

facts.fact: Important animation safeguard: the two carbons released as CO₂ during the first turn are not the newly arriving acetyl carbons. Do not highlight two incoming carbon dots and immediately animate those same dots leaving; acetyl carbons are released on later turns. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/concepts-biology/pages/4-3-citric-acid-cycle-and-oxidative-phosphorylation?utm_source=openai))
facts.when: Source published April 25, 2013; carbon tracing across successive turns.

story.style: 60-second widescreen explainer in simple, clean 2D animation using textbook-style diagrams; calm English narration; no music.
story.story:
Under “Citric acid cycle,” an oval mitochondrial cutaway shows a symbolic, arrow-linked loop in the matrix. Labels identify molecules as calm English narration follows the reactions. Acetyl-CoA supplies a two-carbon acetyl group to four-carbon oxaloacetate, forming six-carbon citrate; CoA-SH is released.

Citrate rearranges into six-carbon isocitrate. Isocitrate becomes five-carbon α-ketoglutarate: CO₂ leaves and the first NADH appears. Next, four-carbon succinyl-CoA forms, releasing a second CO₂ and producing a second NADH. The departing carbons are not the newly arrived acetyl carbons.

Succinyl-CoA becomes succinate, releasing CoA-SH; a GTP → ATP callout represents one ATP equivalent, not two additional products. Membrane-embedded succinate dehydrogenase converts succinate to fumarate as FAD becomes FADH₂. Water enters as fumarate becomes malate.

Malate becomes oxaloacetate, producing the third NADH. The regenerated oxaloacetate can accept another acetyl group, closing the loop. The completed turn shows two CO₂, three NADH, one FADH₂ and one ATP equivalent.
